newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - Telecoms firms tap growing Vietnam market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Telecoms firms tap growing Vietnam market.

text.p: A decade ago telephoning overseas from behind the closed doors of Vietnam was near impossible. The few calls that did get through were routed via satellite through a rickety network in Moscow.
In the late 1980s, the Australian firm Telstra was hired to establish the first reliable link, with a small satellite earth station that transmitted calls to Australia and then to the outside world.
"When our company first arrived in Vietnam there was an argument over whether we should provide capacity for six or nine simultaneous international calls," recalls Business Manager Peter Allan.
"Connections took hours and because the domestic network was so unreliable they could only be made from the post office of Ho Chi Minh City.
TIMES HAVE CHANGED

Today, satellite connections and an undersea fibre-optic cable can carry tens of thousands of international calls. Overseas call minutes will reach nearly 300 million this year, up seven times from the number in 1992.
Explosive growth has also been seen in domestic services. The network reached one million lines in August this year. In 1992 there were only 120,000 customers nationwide.
Three mobile phone networks alone boast about 50,000 subscribers, a number that has doubled in 1996.

While Vietnam still trails other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in phone penetration, it was rated in 1994 by the Swiss-based International Telecommunications Union as the second fastest growing market in the world.
The quality of service has changed too.
Telstra's Allen recalls that "just a few years ago, the domestic network was so unreliable that companies in Ho Chi Minh City would call Hong Kong to get transferred to their Hanoi office."
Now, cities the length of Vietnam are connected by a 2.5 gigabyte fibre-optic backbone, the completion of which was announced by Nortel in Ho Chi Minh City on October 24.
Like most of the country's telecom investments, the backbone is aimed at the needs of the 21st century.
"Vietnam is the first country in the ASEAN region to use this kind of state-of-the-art transmission technology," said James Deas, president of Nortel Asia South Pacific.
DEMAND OUTWEIGHS SUPPLY
Accomplishments aside, the telecom authorities cannot keep pace with demand.

The semi-official Vietnam Investment Review reported recently that Ho Chi Minh City's postal service, which has a monopoly on the city's telephone distribution, has been charging three to four times the government-sanctioned phone line installation rate.
Despite this, about 10,000 people remain on the city's waiting list for a new line. Queues are common in other cities as well.

In the short term, to fill the unmet demand, the central telecom monopoly Vietnam Posts and Telecommunications (VNPT) has signed two contracts, with Hughes Network Systems and Nortel, for wireless local loop networks in Ho Chi Minh City.
Unlike traditional wire-line telephone systems, these wireless networks do not require cable to be laid to the customers' premises, thus shortening installation schedules and reducing costs.
The networks will serve households in outlying parts of the city, where the needs of the fast-growing population have outstripped the existing infrastructure.
Each system has an initial capacity of 20,000 customers, and together could serve up to 160,000 users.
Longer term, the Vietnamese government hopes to increase phone penetration to five per 100 people by 2000, which will require the installation of 2.5 million new lines.
According to one industry executive, this would put Vietnam at the level expected in Indonesia and the Philippines next year.
The expansion would be accomplished through strategic alliances between VNPT and foreign investors, who would bring the technology and the estimated $1.5-2.0 billion in financing.
In a move that industry sources hint indicates the importance of relationships in the market, rather than calling a competitive bid VNPT has hand-picked five firms to install the lines.
These are Korea Telecoms in Haiphong, France Telecom and Telstra in Ho Chi Minh City, and Nippon Telegraph And Telephone and Cable and Wireless Plc in Hanoi.
So far, negotiations for the new fixed lines have dragged on for over two years and only Korea Telecom has signed a contract, though two firms are reportedly close to finalising deals.
Most executives are confident the country will reach its telecoms goals.

Privately, however, they complain that investment conditions are less attractive than in other countries, because of government security regulations that prohibit them from owning or operating the networks.

"This leaves the foreign partners with only technology transfer and financing, whereas virtually everywhere else the foreign operators establish an equity stake and become involved in operations," said one industry executive.
Nonetheless the foreign corporations remain keen.

"Vietnam is a very attractive market for telecom, as there are 75 million people, penetration is still low, and economic growth is high," says Roger Barlow, Representative Director for Cable and Wireless.
France Telecom's Chief Representative, Andre Pietri, adds: "If you want to be present when the economy is big, you have to be active now."
